record.original_question: If variable influence alone is not enough to identify a small set of near-optimal splitting choices when properly learning decision trees, does there exist a slightly higher-order splitting criterion that is still efficiently computable and is strong enough to recover such a small candidate set, thereby enabling a polynomial-time proper learning algorithm?

evidence.quote: Furthermore, this subset can be identified by estimating the influence of each variable w.r.t. f_pi.
If the influence itself is not enough for identifying a small subset of near-optimal choices, would a slightly "higher-order" splitting criterion suffice?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the problem of properly learning decision trees under the uniform distribution on {-1,1}^n in the realizable setting with membership query access. Concretely, let f:{-1,1}^n -> {-1,1} be an unknown Boolean function computed by a decision tree of size s, and let epsilon > 0. An algorithm properly learns f if, with high probability, it outputs a decision tree hypothesis h of size poly(s, n, 1/epsilon) satisfying Pr_x[h(x) != f(x)] <= epsilon, where x is uniform on {-1,1}^n.

Top-down decision-tree learning heuristics (such as ID3, C4.5, CART) work by, at each internal node currently labeled by a restriction pi, choosing a variable x_i to split on according to some splitting criterion S(f_pi, i), where f_pi is the subfunction obtained by applying pi to f. A natural criterion is the influence Inf_i(f_pi) of variable i. Define a splitting criterion S to be "k-th order" if S(g, i) can be expressed as a function of the values { hat{g}(T) : T subseteq [n], |T| <= k, i in T } of the Fourier coefficients of g of degree at most k containing i; such a criterion is efficiently estimable from uniform random examples (or queries) for any constant k.

Question: Does there exist a constant k >= 2 and a k-th order splitting criterion S such that, at every restriction pi reachable during the top-down construction, the variables i maximizing S(f_pi, i) form a set of size poly(s) that contains a near-optimal split (i.e. a split whose use in a greedy top-down procedure yields a decision tree hypothesis of size poly(s,1/epsilon) and error at most epsilon)? Equivalently, can a constant-order splitting criterion be used to obtain a proper learning algorithm for size-s decision trees under the uniform distribution running in time poly(n, s, 1/epsilon)?
artifact.status_search_result: The best known proper learning algorithm for decision trees under the uniform distribution with queries runs in n^{O(log log n)} time (Blanc, Lange, Qiao, Tan, JACM 2022), still super-polynomial. No polynomial-time proper learning algorithm via a higher-order splitting criterion is reported in the literature; the question of whether a constant-order splitting criterion suffices to obtain such an algorithm appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Properly Learning Decision Trees in almost Polynomial Time
status_evidence.snippet: n^{O(log log n)}-time membership query algorithm for properly and agnostically learning decision trees under the uniform distribution.
status_evidence.claim: Current best runtime for proper learning of decision trees is n^{O(log log n)}, not polynomial.

status_evidence.title: Properly learning decision trees in almost polynomial time (arXiv)
status_evidence.snippet: Even in the realizable setting, the previous fastest runtime was n^{O(log n)}.
status_evidence.claim: Polynomial-time proper learning of decision trees remains unresolved.
